## Key Drivers

• **Indian bank stocks sold off on FCNR-deposit and funding-cost concerns** — Axis Bank's CEO warned that record FCNR(B) deposit inflows could fuel "abnormal lending," while rising FCNR(B) deposit costs were flagged as a margin risk for Kotak Mahindra Bank, and reports noted banks left interest payments on roughly $127 billion of overseas deposits unhedged, adding dollar demand and rupee pressure. These are the fund's core banking holdings — ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, SBI, Kotak and Axis together make up a large share of the portfolio — so a sector-wide de-rating in margins and asset-quality expectations was the single biggest reason for the week's decline.

• **A nationwide bank strike on September 11 disrupted sentiment across lenders** — The one-day strike raised operational-disruption concerns for the sector, and it lines up with the weakest trading day of the week for SBI and Axis Bank. Because the fund holds the largest Indian banks, any event that hits the whole sector's operating backdrop feeds straight through to performance.

• **Foreign investors were reported to be reallocating away from Indian financials** — Jefferies suggested global investors may rejig allocations out of Indian financials, implying potential selling pressure on the banks. With ICICI Bank the fund's largest single holding, this sector-level flow risk hit the portfolio's most heavily weighted exposure directly.

• **Bond yields crossing 7% and finance-sector weakness weighed on financial valuations** — Indian bond yields moved back above 7%, pressuring financial-sector valuations and debt-market sentiment, on the day of the week's largest decline. This compounded the drag from the fund's finance exposure beyond the individual bank names.

• **HDFC Bank was a partial offset on a positive governance and sector catalyst** — The board shortlisted two CEO candidates and submitted them to the RBI, with Macquarie calling an external appointment a potential re-rating catalyst, and Moody's simultaneously forecast strong deposit and loan growth for Indian banks. As one of the fund's largest holdings, HDFC Bank's gain softened — but did not reverse — the broader banking drag.

## Overall Summary

The week's decline was driven overwhelmingly by the fund's banking and financial holdings, which sold off together on a cluster of funding-cost, allocation-flow and operational-disruption concerns rather than on any single company's earnings. The dominant themes were the risk of margin pressure and loose lending from record FCNR(B) deposit inflows, a nationwide bank strike on September 11, a reported shift by foreign investors away from Indian financials, and bond yields moving back above 7% — all of which hit the portfolio's largest weights, including ICICI Bank, SBI, Kotak and Axis Bank, at the same time. HDFC Bank provided a meaningful but partial offset, helped by progress on its CEO succession and a constructive sector outlook from Moody's. The takeaway is that this was a sector-wide banking and rates story concentrated in the fund's biggest exposures, not a broad-market event.
